note: Selected pre-Roman Iron Age frame; Celtic languages and identities did not disappear in 43 AD. Stonehenge belongs to the much earlier Neolithic and Bronze Age, rather than to the origin of a Celtic state.

proposedTitle: Lusitanians and neighbouring Iron Age communities
note: An approximate Iron Age frame, not a single kingdom founded in 600 BC. Roman writers attest Lusitanians later; the Lusitanian War ended in 139 BC but regional conquest continued.

A broad grouping of distinct peoples, languages and regional societies. Iberian culture is usually identified from the first millennium BC; Rome completed its wider Iberian conquests in 19 BC, not in 218 BC.
Selected Barcid territorial phase beginning with Hamilcar Barca in 237 BC. Phoenician and Punic settlements predate it; Rome expelled the main Carthaginian forces from Iberia in 206 BC.
An approximate regional Iron Age frame, not one Celtic state. Caesar campaigned in 58–50 BC; southern Gaul had already come under Roman rule.

An approximate early grouping of several languages and peoples. Etruscans were not linguistically Italic, Greek colonies were distinct, and Italic communities continued after the Roman monarchy began.
753 BC and 509 BC are traditional foundation and transition dates transmitted by later Roman historians, not archaeologically proven day-one boundaries.
Traditional republican frame; the Republic conquered territories at different times rather than inheriting all the coloured columns at its foundation.

proposedTitle: Roman Republican conquest and rule in Iberia
wikiTitle: Roman conquest of the Iberian Peninsula
note: Roman intervention began in 218 BC, but conquest lasted into the Augustan period. This is a regional phase of the Republic, not a second Roman state.

sources.title: Roman conquest of the Iberian Peninsula

wikiResolution.canonical: Roman conquest of the Iberian Peninsula

note: The poster marks 58 BC. Caesar’s wars ran through 50 BC, while Roman rule in southern Gaul began earlier.

proposedTitle: Central European Celtic and Germanic communities
note: A regional, approximate cultural frame spanning many communities. These categories are linguistic and historical labels, not one government or an unbroken ethnic ancestry.

proposedTitle: Hallstatt culture · early Iron Age phases
note: The selected Iron Age Hallstatt C–D phases date approximately 800–450 BC. Broader Hallstatt A–B material belongs to the earlier Bronze Age; the culture was not a unitary state.

The Norican kingdom or federation consolidated around the second century BC; the poster’s c. 400 BC better describes earlier regional Celtic culture. Roman annexation began in 15 BC; later provincial institutions continued.
An archaeological umbrella including Cycladic, Minoan and Mycenaean cultures with different chronologies; it was not one empire or an exclusive origin story for later Greeks.
The website already covers the Cretan component. This does not by itself cover all Cycladic or mainland Aegean histories.
Early Cycladic chronology is approximate and distinct from the Minoan and mainland Mycenaean sequences. Added explicitly to make the poster’s Aegean umbrella meaningful.

sources.title: Settlements of the Cyclades in the 3rd millennium BC

note: An archaeological period of multiple mainland palace centres, rather than a single uniformly governed Greek nation.

proposedTitle: Early Iron Age Greece · Greek Dark Ages
note: A conventional archaeological period following palace collapse. The label does not imply an absence of communities, creativity or contact; boundaries vary between regions.
The poster starts this label around 800 BC, combining Archaic and Classical Greece. Classical Greece conventionally begins around 480 BC; city-states were independent and often at war.

posterLabel: Classical Greek City-States · earlier Archaic component
note: An expanded conventional frame covering the earlier portion of the poster’s combined Greek band. The existing site uses the narrower art-historical start c. 700 BC; either convention needs an explicit note.

proposedTitle: Macedonian hegemony · Philip II and Alexander
note: 338 BC marks Philip II’s victory at Chaeronea. Alexander’s Asian conquests began in 334 BC; his death in 323 BC initiated succession struggles, rather than instantly creating stable successor states.
The poster’s Greek column ends at Roman conquest in 146 BC. Hellenistic kingdoms elsewhere continued; 31 BC is a common wider period endpoint, with Egypt annexed in 30 BC.
The destruction of Corinth in 146 BC is a conventional marker; incorporation and provincial organisation occurred in stages. This is a regional phase of the Roman Republic.

27 BC marks the conventional beginning of the principate. 476 AD concerns western imperial government; the Eastern Roman state continued. The poster’s cross-column shape is not a precise territorial map.

Approximate transition after the withdrawal of Roman imperial administration, conventionally around 410. Regional British polities continued alongside incoming and established communities; 500 is not a universal end date.
Approximate settlement and early English kingdom frame. It overlaps British polities, Scandinavian rule and the later unified kingdom, rather than replacing every inhabitant.

proposedTitle: House of Wessex · selected royal phase
note: 802 marks Ecgberht’s accession in Wessex; 829 was a temporary supremacy, not the founding of a united England. The selected dynasty frame includes interruptions by Danish rulers; unification is conventionally placed in 927.
The Norman conquest began in 1066. This selected royal period ends with Henry II’s accession in 1154 and does not mean England and Normandy always had identical institutions.
A broad dynastic convention including Angevin, Lancaster and York branches. It does not describe a single stable government or peaceful succession.
The Tudor royal period runs from Henry VII’s victory in 1485 to Elizabeth I’s death in 1603. Wales, Ireland and England had different relationships to royal government.

proposedTitle: Stuarts in England, Scotland and Great Britain
note: The shared crowns began in 1603; England and Scotland remained separate kingdoms until 1707. Republican rule interrupted the monarchy in 1649–1660, and William III was of the House of Orange.
The British Hanoverian royal period runs 1714–1901, not to the poster’s 1917 boundary. Shared monarchy with Hanover ended in 1837 because succession laws differed.
The United Kingdom was created in 1801, not 1917. Most of Ireland left in 1922; the present state name dates to 1927. The royal family adopted the Windsor name in 1917.
1917 marks the adoption of the royal house name Windsor. It is a dynastic phase within the United Kingdom, not the state’s foundation.

A conventional first-county frame beginning with the recovery of Porto in 868. The first comital line ended with Nuno Mendes’s defeat in 1071. Royal administration and later reorganisation preceded Henry of Burgundy’s county around 1096; this was not an uninterrupted independent state.

sources.publisher: University of Coimbra · Mário de Gouveia
sources.title: Nuno Mendes (?-1071): o último conde de Portucale (2013)

note: The second county is usually dated from Henry of Burgundy’s appointment around 1096. Afonso Henriques’ kingship in 1139 and recognition in 1143 and 1179 mark different steps toward independence.
1139 is a traditional royal foundation convention; Zamora in 1143 and papal recognition in 1179 are other milestones. The kingdom’s institutional and territorial extent changed considerably.
Portugal and the Spanish crowns shared Habsburg monarchs. Separate laws, institutions and overseas possessions persisted; this was not complete administrative fusion.
1640 began the restored Portuguese monarchy and the war for recognition, which Spain accepted in 1668. The restored kingdom continued beyond this war and was not newly founded again in 1807.

The Liberal Revolution of 1820 began the constitutional transition; the first constitution followed in 1822. Civil war and absolutist restoration interrupted constitutional government before 1834. The poster’s 1807 start belongs to the French invasions.
The First Republic began with the revolution of 5 October 1910 and ended in the military coup of 1926; it did not continue unbroken until Estado Novo in 1933.
The authoritarian Estado Novo was institutionalised in 1933 and overthrown in the Carnation Revolution of 25 April 1974. A military dictatorship preceded it in 1926–1933.
A modern country frame including the First Republic, military and Estado Novo dictatorships, and the democratic transition. Democracy began after 1974; the present constitution took effect in 1976.
The democratic transition began in 1974 and the constitution took effect in 1976; the poster uses the constitutional date.
The Suebi established rule in northwestern Iberia after crossing the Rhine and entering Iberia. The Visigoths annexed their kingdom in 585; this was not a kingdom encompassing all Iberia.

The kingdom began in Aquitaine in 418 and shifted toward Iberia. The Suebi were annexed in 585; Byzantine-controlled southern areas remained separate until the seventh century. After 711, remnants continued in Septimania into the 720s.
An umbrella for changing Muslim-ruled Iberian territories, not a single state lasting throughout 711–1492. The emirate, caliphate, taifas and later dynasties overlap with northern Christian kingdoms.

718 is a traditional royal origin date. The court and political centre shifted to León in 910, while distinct Asturian royal claims continued to 924; chronology depends on whether one tracks title, court or territory.
A selected independent royal frame. León and Castile were joined and separated at several points; permanent dynastic union in 1230 did not erase León’s regional institutions.

proposedTitle: Late medieval Iberian conquests and Granada
note: 1238 marks the Nasrid foundation convention selected by the poster. Reconquista is a retrospective, contested umbrella rather than one continuous national war; Christian and Muslim rulers also allied across religious boundaries.

proposedTitle: Dynastic union of Castile and Aragon
note: 1479 marks the shared rule of Isabella of Castile and Ferdinand of Aragon after Ferdinand’s Aragonese accession. The crowns retained separate institutions; this was not instant state or territorial unification.
A composite monarchy under the Spanish Habsburgs. Charles I’s accession in 1516 is the selected start; the crowns and territories retained distinct laws and institutions.

proposedTitle: Spain · early Bourbon monarchy and reforms
note: A selected eighteenth-century reform frame under Bourbon rulers, with a major overseas dimension. The reforms were introduced in different territories at different times; not every reform began in 1700.

proposedTitle: Spain · constitutional struggles and regime changes
note: Spain’s first national constitution dates to 1812, not 1808; the Bayonne Statute was imposed under Napoleonic influence. The period includes restored absolutism, constitutional monarchies, republics and dictatorship.
The regime emerged during the Civil War from 1936 and controlled the whole country after 1939. Franco died in 1975, followed by a democratic transition; the 1978 constitution is a separate milestone.

proposedTitle: Spain · composite monarchy and modern eras
note: Country-level frame that distinguishes the late medieval dynastic union from later monarchy, republican, dictatorial and democratic governments.
The democratic transition followed Franco’s death in 1975; the constitution was approved in 1978. This frame does not imply that Spain came into existence in 1978.

proposedTitle: Frankish realms · Merovingian and Carolingian periods
note: 481 marks Clovis I’s accession, not the first existence of Franks. Frankish realms were repeatedly divided; imperial coronation in 800 and partition in 843 are distinct events.
The western share established at Verdun in 843; 987 is a conventional Capetian transition, not an instant replacement of population or institutions.

proposedTitle: Kingdom of France · selected royal frame
note: 987 marks Hugh Capet’s accession and the selected royal frame. France was not a uniformly centralised nation-state throughout this period.

proposedTitle: France · Bourbon monarchy before the Revolution
note: Henry IV’s accession in 1589 begins the selected Bourbon royal frame. Bourbon restoration in 1814–1830 is a later phase, interrupted by Napoleon’s Hundred Days.
The monarchy was abolished in 1792. The republic included the Convention, Directory and Consulate before Napoleon’s imperial title in 1804.

Napoleon’s empire lasted 1804–1814 and returned during the Hundred Days in 1815. The poster’s long black band crosses countries with different occupation dates and incorrectly suggests uniform annexation.
Three French invasions occurred in 1807–1811. Portugal was not permanently annexed to the First French Empire; the royal court moved to Brazil and Anglo-Portuguese forces resisted.

proposedTitle: Spain under Napoleonic occupation and war
note: Joseph Bonaparte’s imposed monarchy and French occupation faced competing Spanish governments and armed resistance. The whole country was never securely governed as one French province.
A northern Italian kingdom under Napoleon, not the whole peninsula. Other areas were annexed to France, governed by allied states or remained outside his rule.
A confederation of German states under Napoleon’s protection, not wholesale French annexation of Germany. The Holy Roman Empire ended in 1806.

The poster’s label is inaccurate: restored monarchies ruled in 1815–1848 and the Second Empire in 1852–1870. The period also includes the Second and Third Republics, occupation, Vichy and provisional government.
Modern France includes republics, empires and restored monarchies. The poster’s 1946 boundary is the Fourth Republic; the Fifth Republic began in 1958.
The Fourth Republic lasted 1946–1958, followed by the Fifth Republic. This country phase is not a single unchanging constitution.
The 395 division concerned imperial courts and administration, not a clean cultural split. The western imperial title ended conventionally in 476, with Julius Nepos retaining a claim until 480.
Theodoric took control of Italy in 493. 553 is a conventional endpoint after Byzantine victories; warfare and residual resistance continued.
Justinian’s reconquest began in 535; Byzantine rule survived in changing parts of Italy until Bari fell in 1071. The poster’s 553–774 band is only a selected phase, not the full duration.
The Lombard kingdom ruled much of the peninsula after 568 and was conquered by Charlemagne in 774. Southern Lombard duchies continued afterward.

sources.title: Longobards in Italy, Places of Power, 568–774 A.D.

proposedTitle: Italian states · medieval communes and regional powers
note: A regional umbrella for many states, cities and jurisdictions, not one state. Venice, Genoa, the Papal States, imperial territories and southern kingdoms had distinct histories.

Founded in 1130. After 1282 the island and mainland crowns were politically divided, with both claiming Sicilian titles; they were formally combined as the Two Sicilies in 1816. The poster’s 1494 boundary is not the kingdom’s end.

proposedTitle: Italy · regional states and foreign intervention
note: 1494 marks the start of the Italian Wars, not the first division of Italy. Regional states and competing foreign powers continued through the early modern period, with major changes during the Napoleonic wars.
The poster’s 1815 restoration relates to the post-Napoleonic settlement. The unified Kingdom of the Two Sicilies was formally created in 1816 and incorporated into the Kingdom of Italy in 1861.
The kingdom was proclaimed in 1861; Venice joined in 1866 and Rome in 1870. Fascist dictatorship developed within the monarchy; the republican referendum took place in 1946.
A modern country frame beginning with proclamation of the kingdom. The republic dates to 1946, and the republican constitution entered into effect in 1948.
The referendum of 2 June 1946 chose a republic; official confirmation followed in June, and the constitution took effect on 1 January 1948.
A selected late antique migration frame encompassing many groups and political formations. Language labels do not imply one people, one kingdom or an unbroken ancestry for modern Germany.

A broad conventional span used by the Metropolitan Museum; other historians use narrower fourth-to-sixth-century ranges. Migration involved warfare, settlement, Roman service and changing identities rather than a single population replacement.

proposedTitle: Post-Roman kingdoms in the eastern Alpine region
note: A selected regional transition among successor authorities, including Ostrogothic influence and emerging Bavarian power. It is not a single named kingdom founded in 476.
The first Bavarian duchy is conventionally traced to the mid-sixth century; Charlemagne deposed Tassilo III in 788. Later Bavarian duchies continued under different political arrangements.
The eastern realm created at Verdun in 843 developed into the medieval German kingdom. The 962 imperial coronation is a selected transition, not the disappearance of its people or institutions.
Otto I’s 962 coronation is the selected start; some imperial narratives begin with 800. This was a changing framework of many states and cities, not a modern German nation-state.
The royal title was adopted in 1701. Prussia did not cease in 1871: it became the largest constituent kingdom of the German Empire and its monarchy ended in 1918.
A loose confederation established at Vienna in 1815 and dissolved in 1866; it was not a united Germany. The North German Confederation followed in 1867 before imperial unification in 1871.
The German Empire was proclaimed in 1871 and its monarchy fell in 1918. The 1919 constitution belongs to the subsequent republic, not the continuation of imperial monarchy.
Republican government was proclaimed in November 1918; the Weimar constitution followed in 1919. Nazi dictatorship developed after Hitler’s appointment in January 1933.
Nazi rule lasted 1933–1945, with escalating dictatorship, aggressive war and genocide. Territorial extent changed; occupation zones followed military defeat.

sources.title: A history of German parliamentary democracy

proposedTitle: Germany · occupation and two German states
note: Allied occupation began in 1945; the Federal Republic and German Democratic Republic were founded separately in 1949. The poster’s 1945 label must not imply that both states already existed then.

sources.title: A history of German parliamentary democracy

note: A broad modern frame including empire, republic, dictatorship, occupation, two states and reunification in 1990. It is not one uninterrupted government.
The GDR acceded to the Federal Republic on 3 October 1990. The Federal Republic itself dates from 1949; modern German history did not begin in 1990.

sources.title: A history of German parliamentary democracy

note: The Babenberg march was established in 976 and elevated to a duchy in 1156. This was a frontier territory within a wider imperial framework, not an independent modern Austria.

sources.publisher: Schönbrunn Group / World of the Habsburgs
sources.title: The House of Austria – the Habsburgs and the Empire

note: The Privilegium Minus elevated the march to a duchy in 1156. The archducal title was invented in the fourteenth century but officially recognised in 1453.

sources.publisher: Schönbrunn Group / World of the Habsburgs
sources.title: The House of Austria – the Habsburgs and the Empire

sources.publisher: Schönbrunn Group / World of the Habsburgs
sources.title: Almost a crown: The Austrian archducal coronet

proposedTitle: Habsburg Austria · archducal and composite monarchy phases
note: 1453 marks formal recognition of the archducal title, not the beginning of Habsburg rule in Austria (which dates to the late thirteenth century). The wider Habsburg monarchy accumulated distinct crowns and territories.

sources.publisher: Schönbrunn Group / World of the Habsburgs
sources.title: The House of Austria – the Habsburgs and the Empire

sources.publisher: Schönbrunn Group / World of the Habsburgs
sources.title: Almost a crown: The Austrian archducal coronet

note: The Austrian imperial title was proclaimed in 1804, while the Holy Roman Empire still existed until 1806. The Dual Monarchy replaced this framework in 1867.

sources.publisher: Schönbrunn Group / World of the Habsburgs
sources.title: The House of Austria – the Habsburgs and the Empire

note: The 1867 Compromise established a dual monarchy with separate Austrian and Hungarian institutions and shared affairs. Its dissolution in 1918 produced several successor states, not simply modern Austria.

Republican Austria emerged in 1918; democratic parliamentary government was dismantled in 1933 and the authoritarian Federal State replaced the constitutional republic in 1934. Nazi annexation followed in 1938.
The republic was restored in 1945, not in 1955. Allied occupation ended under the 1955 State Treaty, followed by constitutional permanent neutrality.

A modern country frame covering the First Republic, authoritarian Federal State, Nazi annexation, restored republic and Allied occupation. Full sovereignty was restored in 1955, not the first existence of the republic.

proposedTitle: Austria · State Treaty and restored sovereignty
note: The 1955 State Treaty ended Allied occupation. The Second Republic had already been restored in 1945, and the neutrality law was a separate act of October 1955.

The empire was Roman in its own identity. The poster’s 395 start marks a division of imperial courts; Constantinople’s dedication in 330 is the website’s selected frame. The Latin conquest interrupted rule in Constantinople in 1204–1261.

wikiTitle: Byzantine Empire under the Laskarid dynasty
note: After the Fourth Crusade, Nicaea, Epirus and Trebizond were distinct successor powers. Nicaea recovered Constantinople in 1261; Trebizond survived until 1461. This was not one state ending uniformly in 1453.

sources.title: Byzantine Empire under the Laskarid dynasty

note: Nicaea was one of several Byzantine successor states after 1204. Its rulers recovered Constantinople in 1261, rather than founding an unrelated empire.
An approximate successor-state frame; the conventional name is retrospective and political control changed. Ottoman conquest of the last Tocco-held territories in 1479 is a conventional endpoint.
The Komnenian empire on the Black Sea survived Constantinople’s fall in 1453 and was conquered by the Ottomans in 1461.
The crusader-founded Latin Empire occupied Constantinople after the Fourth Crusade. It was distinct from the Byzantine successor states and ended there with the city’s recovery in 1261.

proposedTitle: Latin states in the Greek world
note: A broad, non-unitary regional category for Latin and Venetian rule after the Fourth Crusade. Different territories had different durations; some Venetian Ionian possessions survived until 1797. The poster’s tiny band cannot represent one uniform state.

proposedTitle: Kingdom of Greece · first royal phase
note: The monarchy was established in 1832 after the independence struggle and international recognition. Borders expanded later; the Second Hellenic Republic replaced the monarchy in 1924.
The republic lasted 1924–1935 and faced coups and instability. Monarchy was restored in 1935.
The restored royal period included Metaxas dictatorship, Axis occupation, civil war and the 1967 military coup. The junta abolished the monarchy in 1973; democratic institutions returned in 1974.

Independence was internationally recognised in 1830 and the kingdom established in 1832. The democratic Third Republic dates to 1974, with its constitution in 1975; the poster’s 1973 marker refers to a junta-controlled abolition of monarchy.
The junta proclaimed a republic in 1973, but democratic transition began in July 1974; a free December 1974 referendum rejected monarchy and the constitution followed in June 1975.

wikiTitle: Byzantine Empire under the Palaiologos dynasty
note: Michael VIII recovered Constantinople in 1261. The restored empire occupied a reduced and changing territory and ended in Constantinople in 1453; some Byzantine successor territories survived later.

sources.title: Byzantine Empire under the Palaiologos dynasty
